item.content:encoded:
C++ Optimizations in MSVC Build Tools 14.52

The Microsoft C++ team implemented new optimizations in MSVC Build Tools 14.52. Let’s walk through examples of some of these optimizations. We will focus on reassociation, loop optimizations, SIMD code generation, inlining, and patterns. Where noted, we’ll also include a few optimizations that appeared in MSVC 14.51 but which were not covered in previous blog posts.

Improved Reassociation

We improved arithmetic reassociation to make shared calculations easier to identify and eliminate. The compiler is free to reassociate integer expressions and can reassociate floating-point expressions with /fp:fast. Previously, the compiler reassociated terms that would simplify, such as x + y - x, and then rebuilt a balanced expression tree. For example:

(((((a + b) + x) + y) - x) + z) => (a + b) + (y + z)

Although this is good, simplification and balancing alone without regard for common expressions can prevent other optimizations.

Consider this function:

void foo(double x, double y, double z, double d, double* out) {
    out[0] = 1.0 + 2.5 * x * x - d;
    out[1] = 1.0 + 2.5 * y * y - d;
    out[2] = 1.0 + 2.5 * z * z - d;
}

Nothing directly simplifies and there are three addition/subtraction terms so balancing does not do anything, but all three expressions contain 1.0 - d. Under /fp:fast, the compiler should arrange for 1.0 - d to occur once:

void foo(double x, double y, double z, double d, double* out) {
    double temp = 1.0 - d;
    out[0] = temp + 2.5 * x * x;
    out[1] = temp + 2.5 * y * y;
    out[2] = temp + 2.5 * z * z;
}

The updated compiler performs this reassociation. It groups subexpressions in a ranked order where literals come first, followed by loop invariants, then variants. Grouping invariants next to literals, which are also invariant, helps the compiler to hoist larger expressions from loops. Within the groups, the global frequency of each term is considered, including instances where the term occurs with a different sign. Our algorithm is very similar to the one described in the global reassociation section of the paper Effective Partial Redundancy Elimination by Briggs and Cooper.

For example:

void foo2(int n, int x, int* out, int* out2) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        out[i] = 1 + 2 * i + x;
        out2[i] = 1 - 2 * i + x;
    }
}

Applying reassociation, hoisting, and common subexpression elimination yields:

void foo2(int n, int x, int* out, int* out2) {
    int hoisted = 1 + x;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        int temp = 2 * i;
        out[i] = hoisted + temp;
        out2[i] = hoisted - temp;
    }
}

Loop Optimizations

Loop final value optimization

The loop optimizer can replace a repeated induction variable update with a calculation of its final value. When the intermediate values are not needed inside the loop, the updates can be removed. If nothing else remains in the loop, then the loop itself can be removed.

For example, a constant increment repeated a known number of times:

result = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    result += 5;
}

can become:

result = 50;

Other work in the loop does not necessarily prevent final-value optimization. In this example, printing still requires iteration, but updating result does not:

result = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    print(i);
    result += 5;
}

The transformed code keeps the printing loop and materializes the result afterward:

for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    print(i);
}
result = 50;

A runtime trip count can also be handled:

result = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    result += 5;
}

becomes:

result = n > 0 ? n * 5 : 0;

The zero-trip case is preserved. These transformations assume that the compiler can establish the conditions needed to preserve the original program’s behavior.

Better address modes in loops

Address calculations are now optimized with more information about the entire loop, rather than choosing the largest addressing mode for each instruction in isolation. The work spans arithmetic-expression reordering, loop-invariant code motion, common-subexpression elimination, and address-mode construction. The optimization was motivated by unrolled loops where nearby memory accesses can share a common base address. It is especially useful on ARM64, where neighboring loads with a common base can be combined into load-pair (LDP) instructions. For example, consider this sequence of instructions within a loop:

add x28, x8, #1
add x24, x8, #2
add x27, x8, #3
add x20, x8, #4
add x19, x8, #5
add x15, x8, #6
add x23, x8, #7
add x26, x8, #8
add x22, x8, #9
add x14, x8, #10
add x0, x8, #11
add x13, x8, #12
add x1, x8, #13
add x12, x8, #14
add x7, x8, #15
add x11, x8, #16
add x21, x8, #17
add x25, x8, #18

The loop then used 19 individual indexed loads:

ldr d26, [x10, x28, lsl #3]
ldr d25, [x10, x8, lsl #3]
ldr d23, [x10, x24, lsl #3]
ldr d15, [x10, x27, lsl #3]
ldr d14, [x10, x20, lsl #3]
ldr d13, [x10, x19, lsl #3]
ldr d12, [x10, x15, lsl #3]
ldr d0, [x10, x23, lsl #3]
ldr d1, [x10, x26, lsl #3]
ldr d30, [x10, x22, lsl #3]
ldr d29, [x10, x14, lsl #3]
ldr d2, [x10, x0, lsl #3]
ldr d3, [x10, x13, lsl #3]
ldr d4, [x10, x1, lsl #3]
ldr d28, [x10, x12, lsl #3]
ldr d5, [x10, x7, lsl #3]
ldr d6, [x10, x11, lsl #3]
ldr d7, [x10, x21, lsl #3]
ldr d31, [x10, x25, lsl #3]

The improved code calculates a shared base before the loop:

lsl x24, x8, #3
add x28, x24, x10

The loads in the loop use constant offsets from that base, allowing nine pairs and one remaining individual load:

ldp d25, d26, [x28]
ldp d23, d15, [x28, #16]
ldp d14, d13, [x28, #32]
ldp d12, d0, [x28, #48]
ldp d1, d30, [x28, #64]
ldp d29, d2, [x28, #80]
ldp d3, d4, [x28, #96]
ldp d28, d5, [x28, #112]
ldp d6, d7, [x28, #128]
ldr d31, [x28, #144]

Sharing ARM64 address calculations across indexed accesses

Another address-mode improvement targets accesses that share a fixed member offset but use different array indices, such as as neighborhood-pattern computation that loads eight elements from a member array. Each address has the form:

(basePtr + varyingIndex * elementSize) + memberOffset

Previously, the compiler calculated basePtr + varyingIndex * elementSize separately for each access and folded memberOffset into the load. Although each address mode was efficient in isolation, the sequence repeated work.

The improved code instead computes a shared base:

sharedBase = basePtr + memberOffset
address = sharedBase + varyingIndex * elementSize

For example, the old ARM64 sequence contained eight address calculations and eight loads. The first two accesses looked like this:

add x8, x19, x10, lsl #2
ldr w0, [x8, #0x500]
add x8, x19, x11, lsl #2
ldr w1, [x8, #0x500]

With the member offset included in a shared base, all eight loads can use scaled-indexed addressing directly:

add x20, x19, #0x500
ldr w0, [x20, x10, lsl #2]
ldr w1, [x20, x11, lsl #2]
ldr w2, [x20, x12, lsl #2]
ldr w3, [x20, x13, lsl #2]
ldr w4, [x20, x14, lsl #2]
ldr w5, [x20, x15, lsl #2]
ldr w6, [x20, x16, lsl #2]
ldr w7, [x20, x17, lsl #2]

This reduces the sequence from 16 instructions to nine. Unlike the preceding load-pair example, the indices can differ; the opportunity is to share the fixed part of the address, not to combine adjacent loads.

Hoisting conditionally executed loop-invariant operations

Loop-invariant code motion can now hoist eligible pure operations even when they originally appeared in a conditional block. The inputs do not change between iterations, so the calculation need not be repeated whenever the condition is true.

For example:

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    if (i % 2) {
        sum += a * b;
    }
}

can be transformed into:

c = a * b;
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    if (i % 2) {
        sum += c;
    }
}

The multiplication moves out of the loop and the conditional accumulation stays in place. This is not a general license to move side effects or unsafe operations out of conditional execution.

SIMD Code Generation and Vectorization

Small-loop vectorization on ARM64

Starting in MSVC 14.51, the ARM64 loop vectorizer accepts small loops that exactly fill a vector register, including 64-bit vectors. Previously, a loop such as this was rejected as too small:

void small_loop(int* __restrict a, const int* __restrict b) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) {
        a[i] += b[i];
    }
}

Now the loop body vectorizes as:

ldr d17, [x0]
ldr d16, [x1]
add v16.2s, v17.2s, v16.2s
str d16, [x0]

ARM64 NEON bitmask patterns

The first pattern combines negation with a sign test when range information proves the input to the negation cannot be INT_MIN. For example:

#include <arm_neon.h>

int32x4_t shift_sign_bit_s32(int32x4_t a) {
    return vshrq_n_s32(vnegq_s32(vshrq_n_s32(a, 1)), 31);
}

In MSVC 14.50, the sequence was:

sshr v16.4s, v0.4s, #1
neg v16.4s, v16.4s
cmlt v0.4s, v16.4s, #0

In MSVC 14.51, the initial shift supplies the range information needed to replace the last two instructions with a positive comparison:

sshr v16.4s, v0.4s, #1
cmgt v0.4s, v16.4s, #0

The second pattern tests whether all bits above the low byte are zero:

#include <arm_neon.h>

int32x4_t test_int32_t(int32x4_t a) {
    return vceqq_s32(vandq_s32(a, vdupq_n_s32(-256)), vdupq_n_s32(0));
}

The literal mask-and-compare implementation in MSVC 14.50:

mvni v16.4s, #0xFF
movi v17.4s, #0
and v16.16b, v0.16b, v16.16b
cmeq v0.4s, v16.4s, v17.4s

is replaced in MSVC 14.51 with an unsigned comparison against 256:

movi v16.4s, #1, lsl #8
cmhi v0.4s, v16.4s, v0.4s

ARM64 NEON pairwise add-and-accumulate patterns

The compiler recognizes a widening pairwise addition followed by accumulation:

#include <arm_neon.h>

uint32x4_t test_uint32x4(uint32x4_t acc, uint16x8_t a) {
    const auto pairs = vpaddlq_u16(a);
    return vaddq_u32(acc, pairs);
}

Instead of the two instructions emitted by MSVC 14.50:

uaddlp v16.4s, v1.8h
add v0.4s, v0.4s, v16.4s

14.51 emits:

uadalp v0.4s, v1.8h

The signed variant similarly uses SADALP.

SLP recognition of scalar reductions

In MSVC 14.51, superword-level parallelism (SLP) vectorization can recognize scalar reductions such as:

int reduce(const int* a) {
    return a[0] + a[1] + a[2] + a[3];
}

ARM64 has a horizontal sum instruction that makes this compact:

ldr q16, [x0]
addv s16, v16.4s

On x64, reducing vector lanes requires a larger sequence. The profitability decision therefore also considers whether other vectorizable operations can offset the reduction cost.

SLP recognition of phi nodes

In MSVC 14.52, SLP can vectorize phi nodes, extending its scope beyond straight-line basic blocks to patterns involving loops. For example, consider two neighboring accumulations:

#include <stdint.h>

void slp_phi(int64_t* dst, const int64_t* src, int n) {
    int64_t a = 0;
    int64_t b = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i += 2) {
        a += src[i];
        b += src[i + 1];
    }
    dst[0] = a;
    dst[1] = b;
}

These can be processed as two vector lanes. In static single assignment form, phi nodes merge the initial accumulator values with the values produced by previous loop iterations. Recognizing those nodes allows SLP to follow the accumulations through the loop, rather than stopping at the merge.

The transformation can be illustrated with vectorized SSA pseudocode:

a_0 = broadcast(0)
for (i = 0; i < n; i += 2):
    a_1 = phi(a_0, a_2)
    a_2 = a_1 + load(&src[i])
a_3 = phi(a_0, a_2)
store(&dst[0], a_3)

Recognizing adjacent data through address arithmetic

In MSVC 14.52, SLP can recognize more neighboring scalar loads and stores even when their addresses are written differently. A motivating example accessed pairs of double values using an index calculated at runtime:

int j = 3 * indices[k];
double dx = xi - x[j];
double dy = yi - x[j + 1];
double r2 = dx * dx + dy * dy;
double scale = 1.0 / (r2 * r2);
double fx = scale * dx;
double fy = scale * dy;
f[j] -= fx;
f[j + 1] -= fy;

To vectorize the neighboring operations, SLP must establish that their memory accesses are adjacent. For an eight-byte double, it can analyze the second address as:

x + (j + 1) * 8  ->  x + j * 8 + 8

Both accesses then have the same variable part, x + j * 8, with byte offsets of zero and eight.

The address builder already supported this distribution when optimizing address expressions. The change makes it available in analysis-only mode too, so SLP can record the constant byte offset and prove adjacency without rewriting the intermediate representation. This applies to both the x loads and the f updates.

For example, updating the two force components separately on ARM64 requires two loads, two subtractions, and two stores:

; x0 = &f[j], d0 = fx, d1 = fy
ldr d2, [x0]
ldr d3, [x0, #8]
fsub d2, d2, d0
fsub d3, d3, d1
str d2, [x0]
str d3, [x0, #8]

With both components in a vector register, the update becomes:

; x0 = &f[j], v0.2d = {fx, fy}
ldr q2, [x0]
fsub v2.2d, v2.2d, v0.2d
str q2, [x0]

Optimizing explicit NEON loads and stores

In MSVC 14.52, explicit NEON load and store intrinsics are canonicalized into generic memory operations. Previously, the compiler kept the specific intrinsics throughout the optimizer, but they did not match existing optimization patterns that expected normal loads and stores. Canonicalizing the NEON loads and stores allowed existing optimizations to apply to them. Ultimately, if the loads and stores persist after optimization, they may become NEON loads and stores again.

Combining scalar stores when constructing vectors

MSVC 14.52 extends scalar-store combining to more data types and ARM64 NEON. When scalar assignments construct a vector that is subsequently loaded as a whole, the compiler can build the value directly in registers rather than storing each component to the stack and loading it back.

For example:

#include <arm_neon.h>

float32x4_t make_vector(float a, float b, float c, float d) {
    float32x4_t result;
    result.n128_f32[0] = a;
    result.n128_f32[1] = b;
    result.n128_f32[2] = c;
    result.n128_f32[3] = d;
    return result;
}

The register-only construction can use lane inserts:

ins v0.s[1], v1.s[0]
ins v0.s[2], v2.s[0]
ins v0.s[3], v3.s[0]

This small example already stayed in registers in MSVC 14.51. The improvement is in larger functions, where control flow and register pressure previously prevented the register allocator from eliminating the temporary stack storage. Combining the stores earlier also exposes the vector to later SIMD optimizations.

More robust bit-pattern recognition

MSVC 14.52 improves the cost model for recognizing scalar bit-manipulation patterns when their inputs are defined in another basic block. For example, this sequence reverses the bits of a 32-bit value:

#include <intrin.h>

unsigned int reverse_bits(unsigned int x) {
    x = ((x & 0x55555555u) << 1) | ((x & 0xAAAAAAAAu) >> 1);
    x = ((x & 0x33333333u) << 2) | ((x & 0xCCCCCCCCu) >> 2);
    x = ((x & 0x0F0F0F0Fu) << 4) | ((x & 0xF0F0F0F0u) >> 4);
    return _byteswap_ulong(x);
}

On ARM64, the calculation can become:

rbit w0, w0

The isolated pattern was already recognized. The new behavior makes recognition more reliable inside large functions with more complicated control flow.

ARM64 NEON arithmetic with a selected lane

A vector multiplication by a broadcast lane no longer needs a separate duplicate instruction when the arithmetic instruction can select that lane directly:

#include <arm_neon.h>

float32x4_t multiply_by_lane(float32x4_t a, float32x4_t b) {
    return vmulq_f32(a, vdupq_laneq_f32(b, 1));
}

MSVC 14.51 emitted:

dup v16.4s, v1.s[1]
fmul v0.4s, v0.4s, v16.4s

MSVC 14.52 folds the broadcast into the multiply:

fmul v0.4s, v0.4s, v1.s[1]

The same recognition applies to fused multiply-add and multiply-subtract, using the by-element forms of FMLA and FMLS. With /fp:fast, the compiler can also exchange the multiplicands to expose these forms when the broadcast appears on the other side of the multiplication.

ARM64 NEON shifted bit-clear patterns

The compiler can combine a mask and shift by moving the mask after the shift and expressing it as an immediate bit-clear operation:

#include <arm_neon.h>

int32x4_t mask_and_shift(int32x4_t a) {
    return vshlq_n_s32(vandq_s32(a, vdupq_n_s32(2)), 30);
}

Previously, this required loading the mask, applying it, and shifting:

movi v16.4s, #2
and v16.16b, v0.16b, v16.16b
shl v0.4s, v16.4s, #30

MSVC 14.52 instead emits:

shl v0.4s, v0.4s, #30
bic v0.4s, #0x40, lsl #24

The shifted result can contain only bits 30 and 31. Clearing bit 30 leaves exactly the bit selected by the original mask, without materializing a vector constant.

Removing masks made redundant by a shift

In related cases, the mask can disappear entirely:

#include <arm_neon.h>

int32x4_t move_low_bit(int32x4_t a) {
    return vshlq_n_s32(vandq_s32(a, vdupq_n_s32(1)), 31);
}

Only the original low bit survives a 31-bit left shift, so masking off the other bits beforehand does not affect the result. Instead of a MOVI, AND, and SHL, MSVC 14.52 needs only:

shl v0.4s, v0.4s, #31

Removing work in unused NEON lanes

MSVC 14.52 tracks which vector lanes are observed and can remove instructions that define only unused lanes. For example, if code inserts zero into lane 3 before an integer vector addition, but subsequently consumes only lanes 0 through 2, the insertion is unnecessary:

; Before
ins v0.s[3], wzr
add v16.4s, v0.4s, v1.4s

; After
add v16.4s, v0.4s, v1.4s

This requires that the remaining operations can safely compute values in the unused lanes.

The compiler also takes advantage of scalar floating-point and NEON values sharing the same physical registers. A broadcast is unnecessary if only the original low lane is used:

#include <arm_neon.h>

float add_low_lane(float a, float b) {
    float32x4_t broadcast = vdupq_n_f32(a);
    return vgetq_lane_f32(broadcast, 0) + b;
}

The previous DUP followed by a scalar addition becomes simply:

fadd s0, s0, s1

ARM64 NEON per-lane rotations

Two complementary shifts combined with a bitwise OR express a rotation within each vector lane:

#include <arm_neon.h>

uint32x4_t rotate_lanes(uint32x4_t unused, uint32x4_t a) {
    return vorrq_u32(vshrq_n_u32(a, 18), vshlq_n_u32(a, 14));
}

The unused parameter puts a in v1, leaving the return register available for an instruction that updates its destination. Previously, the calculation used two shifts and an OR:

shl v17.4s, v1.4s, #14
ushr v16.4s, v1.4s, #18
orr v0.16b, v16.16b, v17.16b

MSVC 14.52 can use unsigned shift-right-and-accumulate:

shl v0.4s, v1.4s, #14
usra v0.4s, v1.4s, #18

The two shifted values occupy disjoint bits, so addition gives the same result as OR. When both shifts are 16, swapping the two halfwords in each 32-bit lane performs the whole rotation with one instruction:

rev32 v0.8h, v1.8h

Inlining Improvements

Inlining removes call overhead, but its larger benefit is often exposing optimizations across a function boundary. MSVC 14.52 improves several decisions that previously left useful helper functions out of line. The examples below illustrate the opportunities; they are not minimal reproductions of a missed inline, and small versions may already inline with earlier compilers.

Single-call-site helpers inside force-inline functions

The inliner can give special consideration to eligible functions with a single call site. Previously, this analysis was disabled while optimizing a __forceinline root function, even when its helper was explicitly marked inline.

Consider this call structure:

static inline unsigned mix(unsigned x) {
    x ^= x >> 16;
    x *= 0x7FEB352Du;
    x ^= x >> 15;
    return x;
}

__forceinline unsigned bucket(unsigned x) {
    return mix(x) & 255u;
}

unsigned lookup_bucket(unsigned x) {
    return bucket(x);
}

The __forceinline on bucket does not itself request that mix be inlined. The improvement allows the single-call-site heuristic to consider a user-marked inline helper such as mix while optimizing bucket. The result can expose the helper’s arithmetic together with its caller’s masking and other surrounding work.

Keeping slightly larger small helpers inline

MSVC 14.52 raises the small-function allowance from 40 to 50 instructions. The motivating NEON shuffle helpers were roughly 48 nodes, just outside the old allowance.

For example, a SIMD abstraction can wrap lane selection in a template:

#include <arm_neon.h>

template<int Lane>
inline float32x4_t broadcast_lane(float32x4_t value) {
    return vdupq_laneq_f32(value, Lane);
}

float32x4_t scale_vector(float32x4_t a, float32x4_t b) {
    return vmulq_f32(a, broadcast_lane<1>(b));
}

Keeping such wrappers inline exposes the constant lane selection to the SIMD optimizer, allowing opportunities such as the by-element multiply described above. The example is deliberately small; the allowance change matters for larger wrappers whose intermediate representation falls between the old and new limits. These are compiler-internal size estimates, not source-line counts or a new unconditional inlining guarantee.

Accounting for scalar replacement of local aggregates

The inliner now recognizes more calls whose removal can enable scalar replacement of aggregates (SROA) and dead-store elimination. Passing the address of a local struct to a function forces it to have a memory location, such that the entire struct is written to memory in the caller. The called function might use only a few fields of the struct. Inlining exposes the fields that are actually needed, allowing the optimizer to keep those useful values in registers and skip copying the struct to memory.

For example:

#include <stdint.h>

struct Values {
    uint64_t a, b, c, d;
};

void adjust(Values* values, uint64_t delta) {
    values->a += delta;
    values->b += delta;
    values->c += delta;
    values->d += delta;
}

uint64_t calculate(
    uint64_t a, uint64_t c, uint64_t delta) {
    Values values = {a, 0, c, 0};
    adjust(&values, delta);
    return values.a + values.c;
}

Once adjust is inlined, the struct and the updates to its unused b and d fields can disappear. The useful calculation is equivalent to:

return (a + delta) + (c + delta);

The new heuristic gives a bonus to eligible calls that the normal heuristic would otherwise decline. It combines a summary of the callee’s fixed-offset pointer accesses with caller-side evidence that the argument is a suitable local aggregate. Pointer escapes, variable-offset accesses, and other cases the analysis cannot safely characterize do not receive this benefit.

Pattern-based Optimizations

MSVC 14.52 recognizes additional profitable arithmetic, selection, comparison, and bitwise-expression patterns. The examples in this section use simplified x64 assembly for optimized builds with /O2; the reciprocal transformation additionally requires /fp:fast.

Sharing a reciprocal across repeated divisions

Several divisions by the same floating-point value can share a reciprocal:

void divide_by_common_value(
    double a, double b, double c, double divisor, double* out) {
    out[0] = a / divisor;
    out[1] = b / divisor;
    out[2] = c / divisor;
}

Instead of three separate divisions:

divsd xmm0, xmm3
divsd xmm1, xmm3
divsd xmm2, xmm3

the compiler can perform one division followed by three multiplications:

movsd xmm4, QWORD PTR [one]
divsd xmm4, xmm3
mulsd xmm0, xmm4
mulsd xmm1, xmm4
mulsd xmm2, xmm4

This transformation requires /fp:fast. It is cost-based rather than unconditional: with only a few uses, direct division may be preferable because introducing a reciprocal adds a temporary and can lengthen live ranges.

More branchless selections on x64

The x64 if-conversion profitability decision now accepts nonzero integer constants in a pattern already supported on ARM64. A small selection such as:

int select_value(int a, int b) {
    return a < b ? a + b : 7;
}

might previously use a branch:

lea eax, DWORD PTR [rcx+rdx]
cmp ecx, edx
jl selected_sum
mov eax, 7
selected_sum:

In MSVC 14.52, it instead can select between register values with a conditional move:

cmp ecx, edx
lea eax, DWORD PTR [rcx+rdx]
mov r8d, 7
cmovge eax, r8d

This removes the control-flow branch and its potential misprediction cost.

Collapsing Boolean expressions to XOR

Some multi-operation Boolean expressions compute a simple exclusive OR:

unsigned symmetric_difference(unsigned a, unsigned b) {
    return (a | b) & ~(a & b);
}

A literal implementation might use:

mov eax, ecx
or ecx, edx
and eax, edx
not eax
and eax, ecx

Recognizing the identity reduces the sequence to:

xor ecx, edx
mov eax, ecx

Related forms, including XOR combinations of the AND and OR of the same operands, can simplify in the same way.

Reusing equivalent reversed comparisons

Reversing both comparison operands and the condition can express the same test. Recognizing that equivalence avoids computing identical Boolean values independently:

int equivalent_compare_difference(int a, int b) {
    const int first = a >= b ? 1 : 0;
    const int second = b <= a ? 1 : 0;
    return first - second;
}

Instead of:

xor r8d, r8d
cmp edx, ecx
setle r8b
xor eax, eax
cmp ecx, edx
setge al
sub eax, r8d

the entire expression becomes:

xor eax, eax

Canonicalizing the comparison both enables reuse and exposes the constant result of subtracting equal values.

Recognizing equivalent minimum and maximum selections

Two differently written selections can also compute the same minimum or maximum:

int equivalent_max_difference(int a, int b) {
    const int first = a > b ? a : b;
    const int second = b > a ? b : a;
    return first - second;
}

Without recognizing their equivalence, the compiler might emit:

cmp edx, ecx
mov eax, ecx
cmovg eax, edx
cmovl edx, ecx
sub edx, eax
mov eax, edx

Both selections return the same value, so the optimized result is simply:

xor eax, eax

The recognition covers signed minimum and maximum forms with strict or non-strict comparisons, including equivalent results combined with XOR. Besides saving instructions directly, these simplifications reduce temporary values and can expose further opportunities in later optimization passes.

Conclusion

The Microsoft C++ team released many new optimizations in MSVC Build Tools 14.52. We will continue focusing on performance while developing MSVC 14.53. Many thanks to the compiler engineers who implemented the optimizations and helped write sections of this blog post, including Alex Wong, Aman Arora, Chris Pulido, Reka Kovacs, and Swaroop Sridhar.

MSVC Build Tools 14.52 is available as part of Visual Studio 2026. Try it out today and share your feedback on Visual Studio Developer Community.

item.content:encoded:
Microsoft C++ (MSVC) Build Tools version 14.52 is now generally available as a long-term support (LTS) release. It is available with Visual Studio 2026 version 18.12 on the Stable Channel and Visual Studio 2026 LTSC version 18.11, both released on November 10.

With this release, C++23 is ready for production use through /std:c++23, and the Standard Library is C++23 feature complete. You also get code-generation improvements for x64 and ARM64 and the general availability of C++ Dynamic Debugging.

An LTS toolset for your team

MSVC 14.52 gives teams that want to standardize on a C++ toolset an LTS option in both Visual Studio channels. Stable continues to receive Visual Studio feature and quality updates; LTSC is an option if your organization wants to limit changes to its Visual Studio environment. Learn more in Announcing Visual Studio 2026 LTSC 18.11.

MSVC and Visual Studio have their own support lifecycles. Keep your Visual Studio installation and MSVC toolset current with applicable servicing updates. This release was not scheduled to be an LTS under our current lifecycle, but we added 14.52 as LTS to help C++ workload teams upgrade and stay in sync with VS. We’ll share more about the MSVC lifecycle in a future announcement.

What’s new in MSVC 14.52

The MSVC Build Tools Preview updates – August 2026 post covered work targeting 14.52 across the compiler, optimizer, linker, Standard Library, and related tools. The later 14.52 Release Candidate post has the full change list. Here are a few highlights:

  • C++23 for production: /std:c++23 is now available. The STL is C++23 feature complete; constexpr <cmath> and <cstdlib> support is opt-in with /Zc:cmath. See the STL Changelog and constexpr cmath with LLVM libc.
  • Better optimization across architectures: The preview updates added improvements to inlining, loop optimization, vectorization, and instruction selection. ARM64 benefits include better vector operations and load pairing; x64 gains include expanded APX code generation.
  • APX targeting now generally available: MSVC 14.52 brings production support for targeting Intel Advanced Performance Extensions (APX) in x64 builds.
  • More reliable C++ modules and diagnostics: 14.52 greatly improves the reliability of C++ modules with updates to diagnostics, dependent code scenarios, and better feedback at link time.
  • Libraries and tools: Highlights include SVE-vectorized Standard Library algorithms on ARM64, improved AddressSanitizer performance and instruction decoding, and better handling of large debug-information streams.
  • C++ Dynamic Debugging: Now generally available with MSVC 14.52, making it easier to inspect optimized builds.
  • Community fixes: The preview and RC posts list many fixes reported through Developer Community, including compiler, code-generation, C++ modules, linker, and library issues.

Update with confidence

Step 1 – Install or update Visual Studio 2026 and MSVC

Use the Visual Studio Installer to install or update Visual Studio 2026 18.12 on Stable or Visual Studio 2026 LTSC 18.11. Select the C++ workload and the MSVC 14.52 components for the architectures you need.

Step 2 – Configure your projects

Load your project in Visual Studio 2026. If you are using CMake, check that your configuration selects MSVC 14.52. If you are using MSBuild (.vcxproj) and moving from an MSVC version that came with Visual Studio 2022 or earlier, the Setup Assistant helps you retarget your projects. To open it manually, select Project > Retarget solution. You can also update the Platform Toolset in the project property pages.

Step 3 – Use GitHub Copilot modernization for C++ to resolve upgrade issues quickly

Use the @Modernize agent in the GitHub Copilot Chat window in Visual Studio to speed up your move to MSVC 14.52. It inspects your build for upgrade-related issues and works with you to resolve them, possibly saving hours or days. Learn more about upgrading MSVC with the @Modernize agent on Microsoft Learn.

MSVC Build Tools Previews

To try work in progress, install Visual Studio 2026 Insiders and select the MSVC Build Tools Preview. Insiders receives preview updates more frequently. Previews are not serviced; for a supported, long-lived baseline, use 14.52.

Update today!

MSVC 14.52 combines C++23 for production, improved generated code and a long-term support option. Update today and share your feedback on Visual Studio Developer Community.

item.content:encoded:
The MSVC Build Tools Preview is updated regularly with the latest features and fixes from the MSVC development team. This post covers the last month’s updates of the Preview build tools, currently targeting the v14.53 release. This encompasses changes across the compiler frontend, backend, linker, standard library, and related tools.

Although you can acquire the MSVC Build Tools Preview through either the Visual Studio 2026 Stable Channel or Visual Studio 2026 Insiders Channel , Insiders gets MSVC Preview updates more frequently.

To check if it’s installed simply make sure one or both of these components are checked in the installer:

  1. MSVC Build Tools for x64/x86 (Preview)
  2. MSVC Build Tools for ARM64/ARM64EC (Preview)

Follow the instructions on https://aka.ms/msvc/preview to configure your IDE & command prompts to use the MSVC Build Tools Preview.

The version number printed by cl.exe and link.exe will be at least 19.53.36930 / 14.53.36930.

We appreciate any feedback that you may have. Please report any issues on Visual Studio Developer Community so we can address them by the time we move out of preview.

C++ Conformance and Frontend

  • Added support for [[fallthrough]] in C++14 mode.
  • Added C++ warnings C4878 and C4879 for additional explicit and implicit conversions between HRESULT or SCODE and Boolean-like types. Both warnings are level 4 and off by default. Ticket
  • Added /Zc:__super[-] and /Zc:__if_exists[-] to control the __super and __if_exists Microsoft extensions.
  • Reduced frontend memory usage by improving allocation and lifetime management for buffered source tokens.
  • Added -fsanitize-coverage-ignorelist as an alternative spelling for -fsanitize-coverage-blocklist, preserving compatibility with existing command lines. Ticket

Code Generation and Optimization

ARM64 improvements:

  • Extended experimental support for the Arm Scalable Matrix Extension under /feature:sme, including streaming-function declarations, supported direct and indirect calls, link-time code generation, exception handling, and runtime state-management helpers. Support is native ARM64 only and remains partial; streaming-function definitions and ARM64EC are not supported.
  • Added the ARM64_FPMR constant for _ReadStatusReg and _WriteStatusReg, along with the FPMR register name in the ARM64 assembler and disassembler. Executing these instructions requires hardware and operating-system support.
  • Improved inlining decisions on ARM64 and ARM64EC by accounting for floating-point and vector-register pressure, helping avoid unnecessary spills.
  • Replaced some multi-step NEON zero-extension sequences with a table-lookup instruction.

x64 and x86 improvements:

  • Expanded APX conditional-compare generation, including comparisons produced when lowering switch statements, and improved conditional-move instruction selection.
  • Re-enabled compact x64 epilog generation for unwind version 3.
  • Improved AVX-512 instruction selection by combining supported arithmetic-and-blend sequences into merge-masked arithmetic instructions.
  • Replaced eligible late-stage constant multiplications on x64 with shorter address-calculation instructions.

Optimizer improvements:

  • Added opt-in automatic load-time function selection for link-time code generation. The [[msvc::auto_dispatch]] attribute can generate CPU-specific implementations from one function body for selection by a supporting loader.
  • Improved inlining decisions to expose more opportunities for simplifying aggregate objects and eliminating unused stores.
  • Improved constant-remainder optimization on x86 and ARM64, replacing eligible hardware divisions with multiply-and-shift sequences.
  • Removed redundant comparisons and unreachable branches inside loops when their outcomes follow from the loop bounds.
  • Expanded vectorization opportunities by recognizing more non-overlapping memory accesses and more ways to pack scalar values into vectors.
  • Added partial support for vectorizing groups of three elements.
  • Improved loop-unswitching decisions so more loops can be simplified before vectorization, including eligible conditions read through pointers.
  • Reduced padding in generated runtime type information and exception-handling data, helping reduce 64-bit executable and DLL sizes.

Linker and Assembler

  • Added the opt-in linker option /WARNUNUSEDLIBS. It emits LNK4324 for each input library from which no members were loaded. The warning supports /IGNORE:4324 and warning-as-error settings without changing /VERBOSE:UNUSEDLIBS. Ticket
  • Improved incremental-link performance for projects with large numbers of input files by reducing repeated filename searches.
  • Expanded the set of valid epilog instructions accepted by MASM with unwind version 3, including VERW and SWAPGS.

Static Analysis

  • Expanded C26433 and C26435 checking to virtual destructor overrides, aligning the checks with the current C++ Core Guidelines. Ticket

AddressSanitizer

  • Added the opt-in windows_shadow_top_down option on 64-bit Windows. Setting ASAN_OPTIONS=windows_shadow_top_down=1 before AddressSanitizer initializes places shadow memory in the highest available address range that fits, rather than the lowest. This can reduce managed-runtime memory overhead when loading an instrumented DLL into an application using the .NET Framework garbage collector. The option is off by default, has no effect on 32-bit Windows, and must be set through the environment early enough to affect initialization; __asan_default_options is too late to change shadow placement.

Standard Library

See the STL changelog for details on standard library improvements in the MSVC Build Tools Preview.

item.content:encoded:
Introduction

We are excited to announce that C++ Dynamic Debugging is now generally available in all Visual Studio 2026 channels and the Microsoft C++ (MSVC) Build Tools version 14.52.

In the traditional workflow for games or large applications, switching to a debug build gives you access to debug symbols at the expense of performance. In contrast, when you debug optimized or release builds, you’ll often encounter variables that are “optimized away” and find it difficult to step reliably through the code you want to inspect.

With C++ Dynamic Debugging, you get the best of both worlds. You can inspect local variables, step through your source line by line, and step into inlined functions. The rest of your application stays optimized, so you can keep the runtime performance you need to reach and investigate a problem.

After turning on the feature and rebuilding your application, Dynamic Debugging will deoptimize functions for you when setting a breakpoint or stepping into a function. You don’t need to stop, add #pragma optimize, rebuild, and reproduce the issue again just to inspect that code. For large games and performance-sensitive applications, that means less time preparing to debug and more time investigating the issue.

Customer Feedback

From game development to virtual reality, Microsoft teams have already been using C++ Dynamic Debugging to make optimized code easier to debug. Here’s what they’re saying:

“Dynamic Debugging is a game changer for C++ development. It lets me work in the optimized builds I actually need for large game codebases, while still being able to deoptimize and inspect code and runtime state when it matters. It removes a longstanding tradeoff between realistic runtime performance and a productive debugging experience.”

Michael Buschbeck – Principal Software Engineer, Microsoft Havok

“Performance is critical when developing virtual reality applications, so my team builds with optimizations on. Dynamic Debugging lets us debug that optimized code as if it were unoptimized. It’s so seamless you forget how much it’s helping.”

Bryce Hutchings – Principal Software Engineer, Microsoft Cloud Streaming, Mixed Reality, and Graphics

Try it in your project

For an x64 MSBuild C++ project, select your Release configuration then open project properties. Set Configuration Properties > Advanced > Use C++ Dynamic Debugging > Yes. Then, rebuild your project to get started. This setting turns off Whole Program Optimization. For CMake and other build systems, you can pass the new /dynamicdeopt switch to cl.exe, lib.exe, and link.exe.

C++ Dynamic Debugging also works with Unreal Engine 5.6 and later, with support in Unreal Build Tool and Unreal Build Accelerator. To try it, enable WindowsPlatform.bDynamicDebugging = true; in your target’s .Target.cs file and rebuild.

In addition, Dynamic Debugging is compatible with distributed build systems like FastBuild and IncrediBuild.

See the documentation for other build systems, requirements, and limitations.

Share your feedback

We would love to hear how C++ Dynamic Debugging works for your projects. Share your thoughts by commenting below, through Help > Send Feedback in Visual Studio, on X (@VisualC), or by email at visualcpp@microsoft.com.

item.content:encoded:
Accurate C++ code intelligence starts with understanding how your project builds. Compiler options, include paths, and preprocessor definitions all affect how the language server interprets your source files. A compilation database, such as compile_commands.json, provides that context, so that tools such as go-to-definition and find-references can resolve symbols accurately.

The Microsoft C++ Language Server now brings automatic configuration for MSBuild-based projects to GitHub Copilot CLI, using the same enterprise-grade C++ and MSBuild tooling we’ve developed and refined over years of investment in Visual Studio. This extends the automatic setup experience familiar to Visual Studio users to the CLI, backed by the same proven tooling.

With this, the language server bundles an MSBuild compile commands extractor and runs it automatically at startup when a compile_commands.json file needs to be generated, providing the necessary build context with less setup on your part.

What’s changed

Previously, configuring an MSBuild-based project from the Copilot CLI required either supplying a compile_commands.json file yourself or having Copilot locate and run a configuration skill to generate one. That discovery and execution step added setup time and consumed tokens before the agent could use semantic code intelligence.

Automatic MSBuild configuration brings the deterministic setup experience familiar to Visual Studio users to the CLI. Compilation database generation is now built into language server startup rather than depending on the agent to initiate it. This provides:

  • Fewer manual steps. You no longer need to invoke a separate configuration skill for MSBuild projects.
  • More predictable setup with less overhead. Configuration runs automatically during language server startup when needed, rather than relying on Copilot to discover and invoke a separate skill.
  • Project-aware code intelligence. The generated compilation database supplies the build context needed to resolve definitions, references, and other symbol relationships.

For example, when investigating unfamiliar code, you can ask Copilot to find a function’s definition and identify its callers. Automatic configuration removes a preparatory step between opening the repository and using those capabilities.

How does it work?

When you open an MSBuild-based C++ project, the server uses the same MSBuild tooling from Visual Studio to read the include paths, preprocessor definitions, and compiler options defined in your .vcxproj and property sheets. It uses these settings to generate a compilation database that describes how each source file is compiled, helping the server resolve includes, evaluate macros, and provide diagnostics that reflect your build configuration.

Compilation database generation runs in the background and the time required depends on your solution’s size and complexity. You can check the compilation progress at any point with: 

/lsp logs

This only automates the compilation database. See the quick start for installation and prerequisites, including accepting the EULA.

To configure timeout settings or disable the automatic MSBuild configuration, visit our configuration docs. Changes take effect on the next language-server startup.

What about other build systems?

For other build systems, you can provide your own compile_commands.json or use a skill to generate one:

  • CMake: Ask Copilot CLI to “load project” to use the generate-compile-commands skill introduced in the earlier configuration release.
  • Custom builds: Follow the guide to create a custom build extractor skill.

Share your feedback

To report a problem or suggest an improvement, open an issue in the GitHub repository

item.content:encoded:
This blog post summarizes changes to the vcpkg package manager as part of the 2026-10-16 registry release and the 2026-09-26 tool release. These updates include configurable binary-cache compression, improved cache reliability and diagnostics, Boost 1.92, and other improvements and bug fixes.

  • There are now 2,877 total ports available in the vcpkg curated registry. A port is a versioned recipe for building a package from source, such as a C or C++ library.
  • 41 new ports were added to the curated registry since the July registry release.
  • 806 ports were updated between the July and October registry releases. As always, we validate each change to a port by building all other ports that depend on or are depended by the library that is being updated for our main triplets.
  • 178 community contributors submitted merged PRs included in this release.
  • The main vcpkg repo has approximately 7,800 forks and 27,600 stars on GitHub.

vcpkg changelog (2026.10.16 release)

Tool improvements

  • Choose your binary-cache compression level. Use --binary-cache-compression-level=<0-9> or VCPKG_BINARY_CACHE_COMPRESSION_LEVEL to trade ZIP archive size for cache submission time. The command-line option takes precedence. Leaving both unset preserves the default compression level, and the setting does not change package ABIs or prevent restoration of existing archives. NuGet packaging is unaffected (PR: Microsoft/vcpkg-tool#2125, thanks @xiaozhuai!). For example, select a lower compression level when saving ZIP-based binary-cache archives: vcpkg install --binary-cache-compression-level=1
  • Fixed binary cache prechecks assigning provider results to the wrong packages after filtering the action list, improving cache availability reporting (PR: Microsoft/vcpkg-tool#2112, thanks @miyanyan!).
  • Standardized binary cache upload failure diagnostics to make cache submission problems easier to identify (PR: Microsoft/vcpkg-tool#2105, thanks @xiaozhuai!).
  • Preserved underlying registry errors instead of replacing them with a misleading “<port> does not exist” message (PR: Microsoft/vcpkg-tool#2095, thanks @bugale!).
  • Added the apple platform expression for port metadata, allowing one expression to cover Apple target platforms (PR: Microsoft/vcpkg-tool#2121, thanks @cqundefine!).
  • Propagated VCPKG_SSL_REVOKE_BEST_EFFORT to spawned processes so the certificate-revocation setting applies consistently (PR: Microsoft/vcpkg-tool#2098, thanks @mem16k!).
  • Improved Windows bootstrap proxy handling: if malformed HTTPS_PROXY or NO_PROXY settings cause an invalid parameter error, the helper warns and retries using the current user’s explicit Windows proxy settings, or a direct connection if none is configured (PR: Microsoft/vcpkg-tool#2137, thanks @camillebruckmann!).
  • Fixed NuGet exports to include vcpkg.exe in the generated package (PR: Microsoft/vcpkg-tool#2134).
  • Made x-add-version updates transactional so an error does not leave partially updated version metadata, while also reducing unnecessary work when processing unchanged ports (PR: Microsoft/vcpkg-tool#2050).

Notable port updates

  • Boost: 1.91.0 -> 1.92.0, updating the Boost collection of C++ libraries.
  • curl: 8.21.0#1 -> 8.23.0, updating a widely used networking library.
  • OpenSSL: 3.6.3 -> 3.6.5#2, refreshing the cryptography and TLS dependency.
  • libgit2: 1.9.4#1 -> 1.9.7, updating the Git implementation library.
  • Qt Base: 6.11.1#1 -> 6.11.2, updating the core Qt framework port.
  • Vulkan SDK components: 1.4.350.0 -> 1.4.357.0, with Vulkan headers updated from 1.4.350.1 -> 1.4.363.0.
  • Armadillo: 14.4.1#1 -> 15.6.1, bringing a new major version of the linear algebra library.
  • SDL 3: 3.4.12 -> 3.4.18, updating the cross-platform multimedia library.
  • 22 ports were removed as part of registry maintenance: cppdap, ctp, dx, keccak-tiny, kf5diagram, libfreenect2, qtquickcontrols2, rapidfuzz, sdl1, sdl1-mixer, sdl1-net, septag-sx, shiftmedia-libgnutls, sqlpp11-connector-mysql, sqlpp11-connector-sqlite3, tensorflow, tensorflow-cc, tensorflow-common, threadpool, v8, vcpkg-tool-bazel, and vulkan-hpp.
  • Other minor improvements and bug fixes.

Documentation updates

The following documentation changes were published recently:

  • Documented VcpkgManifestInstalledBaseDir for MSBuild solutions that use manifest mode and build multiple triplets, allowing a shared installation base directory with triplet-specific subdirectories (PR: MicrosoftDocs/vcpkg-docs#588, thanks @autoantwort!).
  • Documented VCPKG_PROVIDED_FORTRAN, including its defaults and how custom triplets can select a different Fortran compiler (PR: MicrosoftDocs/vcpkg-docs#600).
  • Added documentation for vcpkg print-usage, which displays usage information for installed packages (PR: MicrosoftDocs/vcpkg-docs#599).
  • Documented the CURL_CA_BUNDLE environment variable for configuring the certificate authority bundle used for downloads (PR: MicrosoftDocs/vcpkg-docs#587).
  • Expanded the platform-expression reference with the apple and bsd platform families, additional platform identifiers, and the corrected Xbox target condition (PR: MicrosoftDocs/vcpkg-docs#612).
  • Documented --binary-cache-compression-level=<0-9> and VCPKG_BINARY_CACHE_COMPRESSION_LEVEL, including precedence, defaults, accepted values, and compatibility with existing cache entries (PR: MicrosoftDocs/vcpkg-docs#613, thanks @xiaozhuai!).
  • Clarified how a repository-level nuget.config containing <clear /> can remove inherited binary-cache sources and cause authentication failures, with guidance for keeping the authenticated source in the effective configuration (PR: MicrosoftDocs/vcpkg-docs#614, thanks @hoshiizumiya!).
  • Updated GitHub Actions examples to pin actions to full commit SHAs instead of version tags (PR: MicrosoftDocs/vcpkg-docs#617).
  • Updated the maintainer guide with a policy for AI-reported bugs in new ports: report findings upstream, accept upstream’s assessment, and close the new port submission if upstream does not respond within 30 days. The update also clarifies terminology and other maintainer guidance (PR: MicrosoftDocs/vcpkg-docs#615).

item.content:encoded:
CppCon 2026 is a wrap! Microsoft returned to Aurora, Colorado, for a week of talks, technical discussions, and conversations with developers from across the C++ community.

Microsoft C++ @ CppCon

At our booth, we met people building games, financial systems, developer tools, embedded software, scientific tools, and other applications. Some were working with the latest language features, and others were maintaining and modernizing systems that have been in production for decades. Many talked to us about debugging, performance, build systems, or modern C++, and a growing number were experimenting with ways AI can help them accomplish their goals in the most effective way possible.

Attendees who completed our annual Microsoft C++ survey were entered for our daily LEGO raffle. This year’s prizes included some great LEGO sets; a retro gaming console, a retro camera, a mini orchid, and a model of the Milky Way galaxy.

Congratulations to our raffle winners and thank you to everyone who took the time to share detailed feedback.

Our Talks

I didn’t get a chance to attend many sessions as I spent most of my time talking with folks at the booth, but I was lucky enough to get to see most of our Microsoft sessions as they were being developed.

The Journey to “/W4 /WX”: How Hard Could It Be?

Keith Stockdale, from Rare, presented another session in his series of talks on dealing with the sometimes massive fallout from making small changes to your build system. After first establishing why someone should increase their warning level and treat warnings as errors, Keith walked through the diagnostics that show up, and how they were resolved.

And there were THOUSANDS of warnings, many of them previously suppressed through #pragmas or on the command line. Notably, the one warning that seemed to be the most pervasive was C4189 (local variable is initialized but not referenced) which they took from nearly 10,000 unique warnings down to zero! Definitely check this talk out if you are interested in generally improving the quality of your codebase and keeping your sanity intact while doing so.

C++ in the Age of AI: How Visual Studio Is Evolving

David Li and Augustin Popa presented this year’s version of our “what’s new” session for Visual Studio. GitHub Copilot has become an important part of the modern development toolbox, so much of the session was focused on how those features show up in Visual Studio, including AI workflows to modernize your code, reduce your build times, and debug your projects.

But there were plenty of features and improvements that aren’t specific to AI workflows, as well. Navigating your code in Visual Studio is now much faster with the latest versions, and MSVC Build Tools v14.52 (ships in November, release candidate available now) will ship with all C++23 features implemented and a /std:c++23 switch, which will also be compatible with C++/CLI. The team has also fixed nearly 650 bugs across the compiler, libraries, and IDEs since last year’s conference.

What’s New for C++ in Visual Studio Code: C++ and AI Tooling for Your Build, Your Code, Your Workflow Watch it on YouTube!

Sinem Akinci and Ben McMorran gave a rundown on the latest and greatest for C++ users of Visual Studio Code. Our Visual Studio Code users are at the forefront of the AI agentic shift, and a lot of this session focused on how you can easily shift between different agentic experiences, depending on the nature of the work, and how you can customize your AI experience with Bring Your Own Key (BYOK), skills, custom agents, and hooks.

I tend to be a Visual Studio guy so a lot of this information wasn’t as useful to me in my day-to-day, but it was nice to see how excited Visual Studio Code users were to talk about their experiences with all of these new features. I for one am looking forward to the day when all AI tools have an easy-to-use BYOK experience that lets you run LLM inference on local hardware.

Turbocharging Native Code Performance: Compiler Optimization, Profile-guided Optimizations, and Beyond

I did get to spend some time in Eric Brumer’s session on how modern CPUs work, how to use profilers, and how those profiles can be used to optimize your products based on behavior of real users. Sample-based Profile Guided Optimizations (SPGO) is a pretty cool evolution of traditional Profile Guided Optimizations (PGO) and it’s already been deployed inside Microsoft to gain non-trivial runtime performance gains.

If you use C++ for the performance it unlocks for your applications, definitely catch this one when it’s available.

The C++ Safety Issues Your Tools Can’t See

Safety for C++ products has been a hot topic over the past decade, and there have been lots of papers and talks on the topic. Ion Todirel’s session starts by summarizing where we have been and introducing a way to discuss the different meanings of safety and how real issues map to them. One of the biggest points that I love to reinforce any chance I get, is that C++ is not C. Many of the problems that C++ has are things that it gets from its history of C compatibility, but unlike C, C++ has a long history of introducing features that are explicitly meant to avoid many of those problems. The talk closes out with a discussion about the broad solution space available to us and how AI can help us make our software safer.

My Major Takeaways

C++ Language Developments

Folks are really excited for new C++ language features, particularly reflection. There were already a couple of sessions, based on existing reflection implementations, showing really compelling things that can be done with the feature. It has the potential to be as impactful as templates were in how we write C++ code.

Performance is King

When we asked developers what they enjoy about C++, they often started with performance and control. CppCon attendees described building low-latency systems, game engines, embedded software, databases, compilers, infrastructure, scientific applications, and other software where memory use, hardware behavior, and predictable performance matter. They value the ability to choose a zero-cost abstraction when one fits, and to choose writing at a lower level when a problem requires it.

AI Normalization

The past few years have seen LLM-based AI workflows become increasingly common for attendees. It feels like there’s been a significant shift in the past year where people have really started to understand how they can use existing AI tools to complete their work faster and easier. Multiple attendees we talked to had conference badges that said something along the line of, “I haven’t written code in N months.” Folks are exploring new product surfaces, such as agentic CLI experiences and mostly-automated agents. There also seems to be much less friction getting started with AI tools, especially as products introduce BYOK capabilities and AI tools get approved for sensitive environments like restricted and air-gapped networks. I expect more talks on how to effectively use AI tools for C++ users in the coming years.

Thank you, CppCon

CppCon is valuable because it brings together people working on very different software who still share many of the same engineering questions.

How can we understand a large codebase more effectively? How can we improve performance without making code harder to maintain? How can we adopt a new language feature safely? Where can AI remove repetitive work, and where does an experienced developer need to stay closely involved?

Thank you to everyone who attended a Microsoft session, visited the booth, completed the survey, participated in an interview, or shared a project with us. Those conversations help us understand your workflows and pain points, and they help us improve the tools you use to make all those awesome products in C++.

CppCon is adding the 2026 session recordings to its video archive on a rolling basis. You can also follow the CppCon YouTube channel and the Microsoft C++ Team Blog for new videos, companion posts, and product updates.

We look forward to continuing the conversation.

item.content:encoded:
We are pleased to announce the availability of the release candidate for Microsoft C++ (MSVC) Build Tools version 14.52. With this release, C++23 is ready for production use and available through the /std:c++23 compiler option; see below for details. This is the last MSVC v14.52 preview before it moves to stable status and full support. You can download it from the Visual Studio 2026 Insiders Channel. As this is the release candidate, it is now the default toolset installed with C++ workloads in this channel. To check if it’s installed simply make sure one or both of these components are checked in the installer:

  1. MSVC Build Tools for x64/x86 (Latest)
  2. MSVC Build Tools for ARM64/ARM64EC (Latest)

The version number printed by cl.exe and link.exe will be at least 14.52.37025 / 19.52.37025.

We appreciate any feedback that you may have. Please report any issues on Visual Studio Developer Community so we can address them by the time we move out of preview.

Version 14.52 is expected to go stable in November and will ship with the 18.12 release of Visual Studio (Stable Channel).

This post summarizes the work done by the MSVC team between the 14.51 and 14.52 releases. This encompasses changes across the compiler frontend, backend, linker, standard library, and related tools.

C++ standards conformance

  • C++23 language mode: Use /std:c++23 to select C++23 language rules. The existing /std:c++23preview spelling still works and is an alias for /std:c++23. The preview form is now deprecated and will be removed in a future update.
  • Immediate escalation: C++23 immediate escalation (P2564R3) lets eligible constexpr functions and lambdas become immediate when their use requires it. It is enabled in C++23 and later modes; C++20 builds can opt in with /Zc:immediateEscalation.
  • Unicode identifiers: C++23 and C23 modes recognize the mathematical compatibility identifier ranges from P3658R1.
  • Constexpr allocation in modules: Module interfaces can represent constexpr functions that contain new T[n] expressions.
  • Preprocessor behavior: _Pragma works in more macro-expansion cases and is supported under /E.
  • Constexpr cmath: Support for C++ compile-time cmath functions remains off-by-default under /std:c++23 and may be enabled via the /Zc:cmath switch. Please see https://devblogs.microsoft.com/cppblog/msvc-c23-constexpr-cmath-with-llvm-libc/ for additional details.

C++/CLI, C, and language tooling

  • /clr is now available in C++23 and later modes.
  • The opt-in /Zc:functionToObjectPtr switch rejects implicit conversions from function pointers to void*.
  • The compiler now accepts selected constexpr constructor-template instantiations involving virtual base classes. Constructing those virtual bases during constant evaluation remains unsupported, so this is limited to the declaration checks for a constexpr function.
  • In C code, C4815 and C4816 now warn when a structure is allocated without storage for its flexible array member or when a structure with a flexible array member is passed by value.
  • The Linux C++ IntelliSense parser maps C++20 and C++23 standard options to the corresponding language modes.
  • Argument-dependent lookup now handles more names that are not exported from a module, and nested template and module instantiation is less prone to failure.
  • Module serialization preserves class data members and template information more consistently. Type merging also works better when several modules share a header unit.
  • Header units preserve macro whitespace so stringized macros survive a round trip. Module processing also handles types first defined in the global module fragment more reliably.
  • Math intrinsics and math headers now work more consistently with modules and constant evaluation.
  • Caret diagnostics use less memory, and several diagnostics reproduce the original source expression more accurately.
  • Preprocessor diagnostics better identify malformed and nested constant expressions.
  • The compiler handles invalid type-trait inputs and malformed function-parameter scopes more consistently.
  • The compiler warns when overriding a deprecated non-pure virtual function.

Code generation and optimization

Inlining:

  • LTCG now considers which fields of a small return object the caller reads, so inlining can discard work that computes unused fields.
  • Whole-program optimization can favor an inline when doing so exposes parts of a local object and makes unused stores removable.
  • A large outlined loop body can now inline through a small wrapper called from a loop.
  • With PGO, small size-optimized virtual-call targets can be speculatively inlined when the profile, size, and growth limits allow it.
  • The inliner follows function-pointer values through aggregate assignments, preserving more indirect-call opportunities in template adapters.
  • Type-based devirtualization now works alongside profile-guided inlining. Hot/cold information also does more to prevent cold code from being pulled into hot callers.

Loop and scalar optimization:

  • The compiler can move more invariant loads out of loops after proving that each load executes on every iteration and remains safe across aliased pointers.
  • Equality-tested loops shed more loop-carried work, and strength reduction handles more wrapping integer induction expressions.
  • When three or more multiplications share a divisor, the optimizer can compute one reciprocal and reuse it instead of restoring repeated divisions.
  • Copy propagation through aliased fields is on by default and understands known-size memcpy and memset operations.
  • x64 conditional selection handles more nonzero constants and safe aliased operands.
  • Unsigned comparisons and induction-variable ranges now establish more nonzero, ordering, and non-overflow facts for later optimization.
  • Scalar conditional expressions gain more value-equivalence, incoming-value, multiply, and shift simplifications.
  • Calls use restrict arguments more precisely when determining memory interference, exposing more optimization around those calls.
  • The x86 optimizer performs more local and cross-block copy propagation.
  • The compiler recognizes more rotate idioms and dynamic bit-field extraction controls, and removes redundant POPCNT zero extension.
  • Small-aggregate optimization removes padding-only assignments, decomposes qualifying whole-struct loads, and forwards eligible loads through local memcpy operations.
  • Constant conversions can fold without /fp:fast when the transformation is otherwise valid.
  • Earlier loop-invariant motion and broader expression reassociation expose more work to later optimization.
  • Larger functions reuse more repeated expressions. Min/max expressions, mixed-signedness compare diamonds, and repeated vector-element extraction also simplify in more cases.
  • More indirect calls to noexcept functions become tail calls. Static constant arrays can also disappear when their storage is unnecessary.
  • Loop unswitching handles more nested-loop cases before vectorization, while straight-line vectorization handles more merged values.
  • Jump chains and induction variables simplify in more cases without losing useful predicates or signedness information.
  • The compiler emits less attribute data, scans exception regions fewer times, bounds pathological dead-use searches, and processes large chained function expressions in linear rather than quadratic time.

Vectorization:

  • On x64 and ARM64, the compiler vectorizes more code that selects values through branches.
  • Integer reductions such as sum += a[i] - b[i] can be reassociated into a form the loop vectorizer recognizes.
  • On x64 and ARM64, vector loads and stores reach copy propagation and scalar replacement earlier. Full-width vectors remain intact when splitting them would discard useful vector operations.
  • The vectorizer recognizes more adjacent-address patterns and is more willing to pack user-written SIMD values when the result can remain in a vector register.
  • A parameter-derived pointer advanced by a loop is recognized as non-aliasing a local array in more cases, avoiding an unnecessary runtime overlap check.
  • The loop vectorizer handles qualifying memory-only swaps and multi-stream copies, including std::swap on arrays of trivial types.
  • More loop-control expressions shared by a following conditional simplify after the loop.

ARM64

  • ARM64 now shares address calculations across related loads and stores, including array-of-structures loops based on function parameters. This removes repeated arithmetic and creates more opportunities for paired loads and stores.
  • Known NEON constants can be built without unnecessary data loads. Scalar loads, broadcasts, and lane inserts also fold into NEON load instructions in more cases.
  • The compiler combines more NEON construction and lane operations, removes unused lane inserts, and eliminates redundant mask comparisons.
  • The loop vectorizer now handles additional floor, ceil, trunc, and round operations.
  • Tail-call decisions are now made per call, so one ineligible call no longer blocks another eligible call in the same function.
  • ARM64 and ARM64EC inlining accounts for floating-point and vector register pressure. This preserves profitable native ARM64 inlines while avoiding excessive spills on restricted ARM64EC targets.
  • Native ARM64 SVE2 supports code generation and disassembly for lane-indexed svmullb and svmullt intrinsics. Execution requires SVE2-capable hardware.
  • LUTI2 and LUTI4 lookup-table support includes BF16 forms. Floating-point absolute minimum/maximum instructions and Common Short Sequence Compression operations are also supported. Each family requires the corresponding processor feature.
  • ARM64_FPMR names the FPMR register for _ReadStatusReg and _WriteStatusReg; armasm64 and the disassembler recognize the same name. Execution requires FEAT_FPMR hardware and OS permission.
  • Native ARM64 supports __preserve_none and [[msvc::musttail]], including specialized interpreter dispatch. The __preserve_none calling convention is C-only and is not supported on ARM64EC.
  • With /feature:sme, the compiler accepts SME attributes and ZA-state types on supported external declarations. Eligible scalar noexcept calls can perform the required streaming-mode transitions, including selected function-pointer, reference, whole-program, and Control Flow Guard cases. Streaming function definitions, ZA-bearing calls, unsupported pointer forms, and vector or aggregate arguments remain unsupported. ARM64EC is excluded.
  • The native ARM64 CRT supplies the AAPCS64 SME state-management routines for TPIDR2, ZA, and ZT0. Availability depends on processor and operating-system state support; ARM64EC is excluded.
  • On ARM64, the /Zc:cmath math runtime now supports the floating-point environment. This initial implementation reports math errors through floating-point exceptions rather than errno.
  • ARM64 stack layout can reuse slots for locals in mutually exclusive switch cases, greatly reducing the frame size of large switches.
  • Stateless SVE all-true predicates can move out of loops when the usual safety and profitability checks allow it.
  • Proven-dead switch edges are removed before switch expansion, exposing more control-flow and value optimizations.
  • Bitfield operations use narrower immediate forms where possible.
  • Register assignment preserves more adjacent load pairs and makes better spill/rematerialization choices for frequently used values.
  • Used-lane tracking now crosses more scalar floating-point operations, exposing dead vector work.
  • The compiler recognizes more vector permutations, per-lane rotations, and vector bit-clear immediate forms.
  • SVE comparisons and the MATCH/NMATCH/WHILE families reuse condition flags more effectively. NEON-to-SVE bridge moves, upper-lane float extraction, and by-element multiply addressing also produce shorter sequences.

x64 and x86

  • Speed-optimized x64 builds have more strategies for fixed-length memcmp. Eligible copies larger than 256 bytes use the runtime copy path instead of a large inline sequence.
  • x64 removes more redundant zero extensions before jump-table address calculations and lowers unsigned division by a constant power of two to a shift.
  • Constant f64x2 assignments can combine so a later vector operation folds to one 128-bit constant move.
  • 32-bit x86 builds can inline fmin, fmax, and copysign; ARM64 can inline copysign.
  • AVX2 and AVX-512 targets can build wider vectors from smaller register values without a memory round trip.
  • AVX-512 code generation uses suitable VEX moves for intrinsic operands and folds eligible single-use masked arithmetic followed by a blend into one merge-masked operation.
  • Builds using /feature:APX gain more arithmetic and conditional-selection forms, fewer redundant moves and comparisons, and APX-aware unrolling and strength-reduction decisions for scalar integer loops.
  • APX support now spans the ABI, assembler, disassembler, and debugging tools. R30 and R31 are nonvolatile, register assignment treats them as killed across setjmp, MASM and the disassembler handle eligible extended-register encodings, and DIA reads APX register context.
  • APX-enabled x64 code generation can fold eligible operands and makes better spill, recomputation, and fold choices.
  • Unwind V3 support now spans code generation, linking, ML64, DIA, and binary instrumentation. It covers chained runtime-function records, large prologs and epilogs, .PUSHFRAME/.POPFRAME, and stack walking. ML64 requires /unwindv3; compiler emission is on by default only for APX functions, and stack walking requires a V3-aware operating system and debugger.
  • x64 recognizes more condition-code-safe INC/DEC forms, including eligible atomic fetch-add sequences.
  • AVX2 intrinsic lowering removes unnecessary scalar-to-vector moves in qualifying _mm_set_sd and _mm256_set1_pd paths.
  • APX code generation includes more new-destination and memory-operand forms, shorter LEA replacements for eligible INC/DEC and SUB sequences, and broader shift, compare, conditional-compare, conditional-move, and constant-propagation support.
  • All-bits-set vector constants and functions containing paired register operations receive better code generation.
  • Shift-range analysis models the hardware shift-count mask, and adjacent two-element double stores combine more effectively.
  • Under /O1 and /Os, additional pre-allocation optimizations and size-aware instruction costs reduce code size.
  • RDPRU uses its required fixed-register constraints.

Standard Library

See the STL Changelog – MSVC Build Tools 14.52 for a complete list of all of the changes in this release, grouped by features, LWG issue resolutions, bug fixes, performance improvements, etc. Some highlights:

  • The STL is C++23 feature complete now that P0533R9 “constexpr For <cmath> And <cstdlib>” has been implemented.
    • This is initially supported for MSVC only, under /std:c++23 /Zc:cmath. We expect to make /std:c++23 imply /Zc:cmath in a future release, but it is currently opt-in. Clang and EDG support will be enabled when the necessary compiler machinery becomes available.
    • For more info, read MSVC C++23: constexpr cmath with LLVM Libc by Cody Miller (MSVC compiler front-end dev) and Bringing Correctly Rounded Math to Production with LLVM-libc by Michael Jones and Tue Ly (LLVM-libc maintainers at Google).
    • And under /std:c++latest /Zc:cmath, we’ve mostly implemented C++26 P1383R2 ‘s constexpr additions for <cmath>. (No <complex> changes yet.) A few functions are not yet implemented by LLVM-libc (see LLVM libc math status ) and accordingly are not yet constexpr. For double, the functions acosh, asinh, atanh, cosh, sinh, tanh, and erf are missing. For float and double, the functions erfc, lgamma, and tgamma are missing. (MSVC uses 64-bit long double, so we don’t need a third implementation of each function.) As soon as they become available, we’ll activate them as constexpr in future releases.
  • 19 LWG issue resolutions, which are bugfixes in the Standard.
    • We track every LWG issue that’s resolved in the Standard in our STL LWG Issues project .
  • Improved <regex> performance in several scenarios.
    • Special thanks to Julian Müller (@muellerj2 on GitHub) for this ongoing correctness and performance overhaul of <regex>.
  • Added ARM64 SVE vectorized implementations of several STL algorithms.
    • Also fixed regressions and improved performance in some of the ARM64/ARM64EC Neon vectorized implementations that were previously added.
    • Special thanks to Hari Limaye at Arm (@hazzlim on GitHub) for this ongoing vectorization work.

AddressSanitizer

  • Improved runtime performance by removing duplicated quarantine work
  • Use MSDIS (MSVC disassembler) as a fallback instruction-length decoder for interception, reducing “unrecognized instruction” failures. This is on by default and can be disabled via ASAN_OPTIONS=windows_use_msdis_decoder=false . To trace what instructions were intercepted by MSDIS instead of the manual instruction decoder, set verbosity=3 and search for logs prefixed with “MSDIS instruction decoder:”.
  • Runtime performance improvements including heap address caching, more efficient memory-mapped heap checks, and faster allocator flag assignments, resulting in significant performance gains across multiple runtime scenarios.

Build tools and diagnostics

  • The C++ frontend accepts more valid designated-initialization forms.
  • The C++ frontend accepts more deeply nested initializers, and the legacy preprocessor allows larger macro buffers.
  • Code Analysis SARIF output includes rule names, descriptions, and help links by default, plus tags where available.
  • LNK2022 and LNK4227 name the relevant metadata item. LNK4323 explains a missing ARM64EC/native object pair.
  • Incremental linking trims excess growth space from program-database files.
  • The disassembly library recognizes MIPS32 and MIPS64 Release 6 instructions and ARM64 matrix-state start/stop instructions.
  • /analyze:log:format:sarifandxml writes both Code Analysis log formats.
  • LNK4321 identifies duplicate C++ module exports while generating an import library.
  • C5089 identifies the experimental combination of /fsanitize=address with /clr, including /clr:netcore.
  • In C++, two new level-4 warnings diagnose implicit and explicit conversions between HRESULT/SCODE and bool-like types. They are off by default and do not apply to C.
  • The opt-in /PDB4GBSTREAMS option raises the size limit for the PDB global/public symbol-record stream to roughly 4 GiB. Other PDB streams retain their existing limits.
  • MASM and the disassembly library recognize the x86 int1/ICEBP instruction (0xF1).
  • LTCG emits C4744 when extern declarations disagree on type.
  • PE reproducibility improves because the image hash no longer includes the PDB age.
  • Tag-based Code Analysis warning groups simplify ruleset authoring.
  • Debugger clients can release a program-database file handle without discarding loaded data, allowing the file to be rebuilt sooner. Debug information also merges module and header-unit types more reliably.
  • Debug records can identify alternate object names, and type-record processing performs fewer allocations and improves throughput on large programs.
  • Linker and assembler diagnostics are clearer, and malformed object files, libraries, and module metadata are handled more defensively.
